name: Patella
func: The kneecap. It shields the front of the knee joint and acts like a pulley, giving the quadriceps more leverage to straighten the leg.

levels.kid:
Your **kneecap** is a little round bone on the front of your knee. You can wiggle it when your leg is relaxed!

It does two jobs. First, it is like a **shield** that protects your knee when you kneel or bump into things. Second, it helps your big thigh muscle pull better, kind of like a wheel on a rope that makes lifting easier. That helps you kick a ball, jump and climb stairs.

Babies have a kneecap made of soft, bendy stuff that slowly turns into hard bone as they grow up.
levels.hs:
The **patella** is the largest **sesamoid bone** in the body: a bone that grows inside a tendon. It sits on the front of the knee, embedded in the **quadriceps tendon** above and continuing below as the **patellar ligament**, which attaches to the **tibial tuberosity** on the shinbone.

Its back surface is covered with very thick **articular cartilage** and glides in a groove on the front of the femur called the **trochlear groove** (or patellar surface). Together they form the **patellofemoral joint**, one part of the knee.

Its main job is mechanical. By pushing the quadriceps tendon forward, away from the knee's pivot point, the patella increases the **lever arm** of the quadriceps, so the same muscle force produces more turning force to straighten (extend) the knee. It also protects the front of the joint.

When a doctor taps the patellar ligament with a reflex hammer, the leg kicks: that is the **knee-jerk (patellar) reflex**, which tests spinal levels L2–L4.
levels.college:
The patella is a flattened, triangular sesamoid bone with a broad **base** superiorly (where the quadriceps tendon inserts) and a pointed **apex** inferiorly (where the patellar ligament arises). It lies anterior to the distal femur, deep to the skin and the **prepatellar bursa**, with the **infrapatellar fat pad** behind the patellar ligament.

Its posterior articular surface is divided by a vertical ridge into a larger **lateral facet** and a smaller **medial facet**, plus a narrow odd facet medially. The lateral facet matches the higher lateral lip of the femoral trochlea, which is an important bony restraint against lateral dislocation.

The patella is pulled in several directions. The quadriceps pull runs up and slightly lateral along the femoral shaft, while the patellar ligament runs straight down, so the patella tends to be pulled laterally. This is measured as the **Q-angle**. Resisting it are the lateral trochlear lip, the lowest horizontal fibres of **vastus medialis (VMO)**, and the **medial patellofemoral ligament (MPFL)**.

Patellofemoral contact forces can exceed several times body weight during squatting and stair climbing, which is why its cartilage is the thickest in the body (up to about 5 mm).

Blood comes from the **genicular anastomosis** around the knee. Ossification usually begins between ages 3 and 6 from one or more centres; failure of a centre to fuse gives a **bipartite patella**, usually superolateral, which can be mistaken for a fracture.
levels.phd:
Mechanically, the patella acts less like a frictionless pulley and more like a **variable lever**. Its effective lever arm peaks around 20–60° of knee flexion; patellectomy reduces quadriceps extension moment substantially (estimates range widely, roughly 15–50%, depending on knee angle and method), which is why the bone is preserved whenever possible.

The patella forms by **endochondral ossification** within the tendon anlage. Sesamoid development depends partly on mechanical load: in embryonic chick and mouse models, paralysis reduces or abolishes sesamoid formation, and transcription factors such as **Sox9** and **Scx** mark the shared tendon–cartilage progenitor population from which it arises.

Its articular cartilage is a model tissue for osteoarthritis research. **Chondrocytes** sit in a matrix of **type II collagen** and **aggrecan**; the superficial zone fibres run parallel to the surface to resist shear, while deep zone fibres anchor vertically into calcified cartilage. Chondrocytes are aneural and avascular and are fed by diffusion from synovial fluid, which helps explain the very poor healing of cartilage defects.

Patellar tracking is governed by an interplay of bony geometry (trochlear depth, patellar height), passive restraints (MPFL, which supplies roughly half of the restraint to lateral displacement near full extension), and active control by the vasti. **Trochlear dysplasia**, a shallow or flat groove, is the strongest single anatomical risk factor for recurrent instability.

Imaging research uses kinematic MRI and dynamic CT to track the patella in real time, and finite-element models estimate contact stress distribution across its facets.
levels.expert:
**Exam:** inspect for swelling (prepatellar bursitis gives a superficial boggy swelling directly over the bone), palpate the borders, and assess tracking. Check for a **J-sign** (the patella shifts laterally as the knee nears full extension) and the **apprehension test** (the patient resists lateral pressure on the patella), which suggests instability. The **patellar tap** detects a moderate effusion. Inability to perform a **straight-leg raise** suggests disruption of the extensor mechanism.

**Fractures** usually come from a direct fall onto the knee. A transverse fracture with separation breaks the extensor mechanism; displaced fractures generally need surgical fixation, classically with **tension-band wiring** or screws. Non-displaced fractures with an intact extensor mechanism are often managed in a brace.

**Dislocation** is almost always lateral, common in adolescents during twisting sports. It often tears the MPFL and can cause an osteochondral fracture of the medial patellar facet or lateral femoral condyle. Recurrent cases may need **MPFL reconstruction** or bony realignment such as tibial tubercle osteotomy.

**Patellar height** is measured on lateral radiographs using the **Insall–Salvati ratio**: **patella alta** (high riding) predisposes to instability, while **patella baja** (low riding) can follow surgery. Skyline (Merchant) views show trochlear depth and patellar tilt.

Other problems: **patellofemoral pain syndrome** (anterior knee pain on stairs and sitting), **Sinding-Larsen-Johansson** disease (traction irritation at the apex in teenagers), and **patellar tendinopathy** (jumper's knee). The **patellar reflex** tests the femoral nerve and roots L3–L4 mainly.

keyPoints: Largest sesamoid bone, inside the quadriceps tendon
Increases the quadriceps lever arm for knee extension
Lateral facet is larger; dislocation is almost always lateral
MPFL and VMO resist lateral displacement
Patellar reflex tests mainly L3–L4 (femoral nerve)

test.q: What type of bone is the patella?
test.explain: It develops inside the quadriceps tendon, which makes it a sesamoid bone, the largest in the body.

test.q: In which direction does the patella almost always dislocate?
test.explain: The quadriceps pull has a lateral component (the Q-angle), so dislocations go laterally, often tearing the MPFL.

test.q: The ligament from the apex of the patella to the tibial tuberosity is the ______ ligament.
test.explain: It is really the continuation of the quadriceps tendon, so it is also called the patellar tendon.

test.q: Which ratio on a lateral X-ray measures patellar height?
test.explain: Insall–Salvati compares patellar tendon length to patellar length; a high value means patella alta.

test.q: Name the ligament that provides about half of the restraint against lateral patellar displacement (abbreviation is fine).
test.explain: The medial patellofemoral ligament is usually torn in a lateral dislocation and is often reconstructed in recurrent instability.
